title: A study comparing retinal detachment surgery with and without a gas bubble injection before surgery
official: Temporising Pneumatic Supplementary Tamponade (TemPeST): a multicentre, single-masked, randomised controlled feasibility trial of pre-operative intravitreal perfluoropropane gas tamponade prior to pars plana vitrectomy for macula-off rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
summary:
Background and study aims 
The retina located at the back of the eye is an important structure for sight. The macula at its centre is essential for sharp vision used in reading and recognising faces. Retinal detachment (RD) is a sight-threatening emergency where the retina pulls away from the back of the eye. Without quick treatment, it can cause permanent sight loss. In about half of cases, the macula is also detached , reducing the chance of visual recovery. 
Surgery is the only way to fix retinal detachment. The most common method is pars plana vitrectomy (PPV), where the gel-like substance (vitreous) inside the eye is removed, the retina is repaired using laser or freezing treatment, and gas or oil maybe added to support healing. Although effective, vitrectomy is often delayed due to limited resources or the need to transfer patients to specialist care centres. New research suggests surgery within 3 days offers better visual outcomes than the traditional 7 day window. This creates pressure on NHS services, and so there is an urgent need for new treatments that can care for patients while they wait for surgery. 
TemPeST describes a treatment and care plan during the period between diagnosis of retinal detachment and surgery. This involves a small volume of gas being injected into the eye shortly after diagnosis, followed by patients needing to avoid making certain head movements or sleeping in specific ways until surgery. The aim of this is to stabilise the retina and protect the macula while the patient waits for surgery. The study aims to test whether it is possible and safe to run a larger clinical trial  comparing TemPeST followed by surgery versus waiting for surgery alone. 

Who can participate? 
Patients aged 18 years and over who present to Moorfields Eye Hospital or Southend Eye Casualty with retinal detachment (macula also detached)

What does the study involve? 
Participants will be randomly allocated to receive TeMPeST and then surgery or to have surgery alone. All participants will undergo surgery within 7 days and will be followed up for 6 months, collecting information about safety, participation, visual outcomes and how the trial process works. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
All participants will undergo vitrectomy as part of routine care, and participation will not delay or withhold necessary surgery. For participants allocated to TemPeST, the temporary gas bubble may cover the retinal tear and allow fluid beneath the retina to be absorbed, potentially enabling the macula to reattach before vitrectomy. This may limit further deterioration in vision while awaiting surgery and could improve the potential for visual recovery. However, the study is not large enough to determine whether these potential benefits occur.
Participants in both groups may benefit from being monitored closely during the study, although most of their clinical care would also be provided routinely. The outcome of the trial may benefit future patients by determining whether a larger trial of TemPeST is feasible and justified and by improving understanding of the treatment and recovery of macula-off retinal detachment.
For participants allocated to TemPeST, the temporary gas bubble may cover the retinal tear and allow fluid beneath the retina to be absorbed, potentially enabling the macula to reattach before vitrectomy. This may limit further deterioration in vision while awaiting surgery and could improve the potential for visual recovery. However, the study is not large enough to determine whether these potential benefits occur.
Additional risks may apply to participants allocated to TemPeST, who will undergo an intravitreal gas injection and anterior chamber paracentesis, in which a small amount of fluid is drained from the front of the eye to help control eye pressure. These procedures may cause temporary discomfort, redness or bleeding on the surface of the eye. Potentially serious complications include raised or low eye pressure, inflammation, infection inside the eye, bleeding inside the eye, damage to the lens, cataract development or progression, new retinal tears, worsening of the retinal detachment or migration of gas beneath the retina. Raised eye pressure may impair blood flow through the central retinal artery. Complications may require additional medication or procedures and, in severe cases, may cause permanent loss of vision. The temporary gas injection may also fail to stabilise the retina before vitrectomy.
The gas bubble will temporarily affect vision and impose restrictions on travel and anaesthesia. Participants must not fly, travel to high altitude or receive nitrous oxide, including Entonox, while gas remains in the eye.
Risks will be minimised through defined eligibility criteria, assessment of contraindications and delivery by appropriately trained clinicians using aseptic technique. Anterior chamber paracentesis will be performed as specified in the protocol, and central retinal artery perfusion will be checked after gas injection. Further pressure-relieving treatment will be provided immediately if perfusion is impaired. Eye pressure and retinal status will be monitored, including at the additional safety review approximately 24 hours after injection. Participants will receive clear safety information, a gas warning alert and instructions about when and how to obtain urgent clinical advice. Adverse events will be recorded and reviewed through the study’s safety-monitoring and oversight arrangements.
Preoperative positioning may cause neck, back or joint discomfort, difficulty sleeping, fatigue, anxiety or disruption to usual activities. Participants receiving TemPeST will receive clear instructions to maintain a face-down position for four hours, followed by upright positioning, avoiding backward head tilt or lying face-up until surgery. Participants may contact the study team if they experience difficulty. They may stop positioning or withdraw from the research without affecting their clinical care; any difficulties or changes will be documented and clinically reviewed.
Participants in both groups may experience inconvenience or fatigue from additional assessments, questionnaires and follow-up. Visits will be aligned with routine care wherever possible, questionnaires will be kept brief, and assistance and rest breaks will be offered, particularly because participants have impaired vision. Participant materials will be provided in accessible formats.
There is no guarantee of direct benefit, and random allocation may be disappointing to some participants. This will be explained during consent.

Where is the study run from? 
Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
August 2026 to March 2028

Who is funding the study? 
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

interventions.name: TemPeST is a two-centre randomised feasibility study involving 60 adults with a retinal detachment affecting the macula, the central part of the retina responsible for detailed vision. Participants will be scheduled for primary vitrectomy within 7 days of presentation. Patients scheduled for surgery

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults aged ≥18 years
2. Macula-off rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in the study eye
3. Planned primary pars plana vitrectomy repair within 7 days of presentation in the study eye
4. Able to provide informed consent
5. Sufficient visual function in at least one eye to engage with study procedures and positioning requirements

Stratification: By recruiting site and symptom duration
Exclusion criteria:
1. Previous vitreoretinal surgery in the study eye
2. Proliferative vitreoretinopathy grade C or greater in the study eye
3. Giant retinal tear in the study eye
4. Significant ocular infection or inflammation in the study eye
5. Inability to safely comply with positioning requirements
6. Contraindication to intravitreal gas injection
7. Participation or planned participation in another interventional ophthalmic trial involving an investigational medicinal product, device or ocular procedure from 30 days before randomisation until the end of the 6-month TemPeST follow-up
8. Planned primary pars plana vitrectomy on the same day as presentation in the study eye
